title: 100,000 Fake Degrees. 28 Universities. The H-1B Fraud Bust Sending Shockwaves Through Indian America.
excerpt: A former U.S. consular officer says 90 per cent of Indian H-1B applications contained fraudulent documents. Investigators have now seized the evidence to prove it.
body:
For decades, the H-1B visa has been the golden ticket for Indian tech professionals in America. It paid for homes in Frisco, funded college savings in Cupertino, and anchored hundreds of thousands of families in a country that never quite made them permanent. Now, the largest fraud investigation in the programme's history threatens to reshape how Washington sees every Indian application that crosses a consular desk.

U.S. authorities have seized more than 100,000 fake degree certificates linked to at least 28 Indian universities, according to federal agencies including Immigration and Customs Enforcement. The centrepiece of the investigation is Manav Bharti University in Himachal Pradesh, which investigators allege sold fraudulent degrees for as little as $1,400 each — degrees that were then used to qualify individuals for H-1B visas in STEM fields.

The bust has drawn national attention after Fox News aired a detailed report, with former White House press secretary Kayleigh McEnany amplifying the findings. Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton has announced his own investigation into a Dallas-area visa consulting operation allegedly tied to the scheme.

## The 90 Per Cent Claim

The most incendiary figure comes from Mahvash Siddiqui, a former U.S. consular officer who adjudicated thousands of visas at the American consulate in Chennai. In sworn testimony, Siddiqui alleged that 80 to 90 per cent of H-1B applications from the region involved fraudulent documentation or unqualified applicants — including forged degrees, fabricated transcripts, and bogus employment letters, often facilitated by visa consultancies.

India accounts for roughly 70 per cent of all H-1B approvals in recent years, making these allegations a direct threat to the programme's credibility. USCIS has acknowledged it does not track data on H-1B awardees who obtained degrees from institutions like Manav Bharti, a gap that critics say allowed the fraud to persist for years.

Acting ICE Director Todd Lyons added fuel to the fire by disclosing that more than 10,000 foreign students were employed by "highly suspect employers" through the Optional Practical Training programme, with many working at empty buildings or residential addresses.

## The Fallout for Legitimate Professionals

For the estimated 600,000 Indian nationals currently on H-1B visas — the overwhelming majority of whom hold genuine degrees from IITs, NITs, and accredited universities — the political fallout could be devastating.

Representative Chip Roy of Texas has already introduced the American White-Collar Worker Jobs Act of 2026, which would replace the H-1B lottery with a wage-based selection process, require employers to prove they tried to hire American workers first, and eliminate the OPT programme entirely. The bill would also end the use of H-1B visas as a pathway to permanent residency.

"For its nearly forty-year history, the H-1B visa has been abused, allowing employers to routinely sideline American STEM workers in favour of cheap foreign labour," Roy said in a statement.

The timing could not be worse. H-1B registrations for 2026 already dropped 54 per cent from their peak, from 7.58 lakh to 3.58 lakh, driven partly by a registration fee hike from $10 to $250 and partly by USCIS's crackdown on duplicate applications.

## The Diaspora Dilemma

In North Texas, where Indian H-1B holders once made up the hottest segment of the housing market, the mood has turned bleak. Real estate agent Neeraj Gupta, who came to Dallas on an H-1B visa himself in 2000, told Bloomberg his phone now rings with sellers, not buyers. Some clients are absorbing monthly rental losses of $300 to $1,500. One senior IT director holding two homes in Frisco valued at over $1 million each is weighing a move back to India.

Immigration attorney Sharadha Kodem, who practises out of Frisco, described the client anxiety as unlike anything in her career. Many who bought homes in remote suburbs while working remotely are now being called back to offices — or told to relocate. Those laid off have just 60 days to find a new sponsor before their visa status lapses.

The fraud investigation lands at a moment when Indian professionals in America are already navigating a hostile policy environment: a proposed rule that could end Day 1 CPT, a bill to kill the H-1B-to-green-card pathway, and a Supreme Court case that could redefine birthright citizenship for children born to visa holders. Each headline erodes the stability that the visa was supposed to provide.

The 100,000 fake degrees are real. The question is whether the political system can distinguish between the fraud and the hundreds of thousands of Indian professionals who did everything right.

*Sources: Fox News, Ainvest, IANS, Bloomberg, U.S. House of Representatives*
